questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Transit-oriented development
questions.learningObjective: Define transit-oriented development
questions.stem: Transit-oriented development is best defined as which of the following?

options.text: Dense, mixed-use development clustered around transit stations
Industrial zones isolated from residential areas
Rural development with no transit access

questions.explanation: TOD clusters dense, mixed-use development around transit stations. Sprawl, separation, and rural no-transit patterns are different.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What transit-oriented development depends on
questions.learningObjective: Identify a precondition for TOD
questions.stem: Which factor is most essential for transit-oriented development to succeed?

options.text: Abundant free parking at every building
Frequent, reliable transit service at the station

questions.explanation: Frequent, reliable transit service is essential for TOD. Parking abundance, single-use zoning, and low density all undermine it.
questions.hint: Transit service must be frequent and reliable.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Disamenity and the sorting it produces
questions.learningObjective: Define a disamenity
questions.stem: A disamenity in urban geography is best described as which of the following?

options.text: A neutral use with no price effect
A desirable feature such as a park or waterfront
An undesirable land use that lowers nearby property values

questions.explanation: A disamenity is an undesirable use that lowers nearby values. Amenities raise values, and neutral or premium uses are not disamenities.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Sorting of land uses around a nuisance
questions.learningObjective: Explain sorting around a nuisance
questions.stem: Explain how land uses sort around a nuisance such as a factory.

answer.exemplar: Sensitive uses like housing avoid the nuisance and move outward, while tolerant uses like industry remain nearby, producing a sorted pattern with a buffer zone.

questions.explanation: Sensitive uses move away from the nuisance, tolerant uses stay near, and a buffer zone forms between them. This is sorting by compatibility.
questions.hint: Sensitive uses flee; tolerant uses stay.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Buffer zone and the price gradient
questions.learningObjective: Define a buffer zone
questions.stem: A buffer zone around a nuisance is best described as which of the following?

options.text: The area with the highest nuisance concentration
options.misconception: confuses buffer with the nuisance itself

options.text: The densest part of the city centre
A transitional area of lower-value or vacant land separating uses

questions.explanation: A buffer zone is transitional, lower-value or vacant land separating incompatible uses. It is not the core, a premium district, or the nuisance itself.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Building the price gradient from the centre outward
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a price gradient is built
questions.stem: Explain how a price gradient is built from the centre outward.

answer.exemplar: Central accessibility is highest, so land there commands the top price; as distance rises, accessibility falls and price declines, forming a gradient from centre to fringe.

questions.explanation: Price is highest where accessibility is highest, at the centre, and falls with distance. The gradient follows accessibility decline.
questions.hint: Price follows accessibility from centre outward.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Urban heat island mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism of an urban heat island
questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains the urban heat island effect?

options.text: Cities are always at higher elevation than rural areas
Urban surfaces absorb and re-radiate heat while evapotranspiration is reduced
Rural areas receive more solar radiation
Urban wind speeds are always higher
options.misconception: higher wind would cool, not heat

questions.explanation: Urban surfaces absorb and re-radiate heat, and reduced evapotranspiration removes less heat. Elevation, radiation differences, and wind are not the cause.

questions.topic: Heat island magnitude between two sites

questions.stem: An urban site records 32 C and a nearby rural site records 27 C. What is the heat island magnitude in degrees C?
questions.explanation: 32 - 27 = 5 C. The magnitude is the difference between urban and rural temperatures.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Building the price gradient from the centre outward
questions.learningObjective: Compute price at a given distance
questions.stem: Price falls linearly from 500 units per hectare at the centre to 100 at 10 km. What is the price at 4 km?
questions.explanation: Drop per km is (500 - 100)/10 = 40; at 4 km price is 500 - 4 x 40 = 340. The decline must be applied per kilometre.
questions.hint: Interpolate linearly from centre to fringe.

questions.topic: Buffer zone and the price gradient
questions.learningObjective: Explain why buffers are lower value
questions.stem: Explain why land in a buffer zone is typically lower in value than land farther from the nuisance.

answer.exemplar: Buffer land lies close enough to the nuisance to suffer some disamenity, but not close enough to be fully incompatible, so it commands a discount relative to distant land.

questions.explanation: Buffer land suffers partial disamenity, so it is discounted relative to distant land. It is not fully incompatible, but not unaffected either.
questions.hint: Partial exposure means a partial discount.
